title: The Mik'uji'w (Stone Giant)
summary: The Mi'kmaq encounter a stone giant in the deep forest — a creature older than the glaciers, made of the mountain itself.
full_text:
The Mi'kmaq called them Mik'uji'w — the Stone Giants. They were not people. They were not spirits. They were something older than both — ancient beings that had lived in the mountains since before the glaciers came.

A hunter named Tumaq was the first to see one. He was walking through the forest near the Cobequid Mountains, tracking a moose, when he noticed that the trees were different. The birch trees were bent. The spruce trees were snapped. Something large had passed through.

He followed the trail to a clearing. In the center of the clearing stood a figure — but it was not a figure of flesh. It was a figure of stone. Its skin was grey granite, cracked and weathered like a cliff face. Its eyes were deep-set, like cave mouths. Its hair was moss — long, green strands that hung to its waist. And its hands were the size of canoes.

Tumaq froze. The Stone Giant did not see him. It was eating — pulling birch trees from the ground and stripping the bark with teeth that were boulders. It chewed slowly, methodically, like a glacier grinding stone.

Tumaq should have run. But the Mi'kmaq had rules about the Stone Giants: never run from them, never hide from them, never look them in the eyes. If you did, they would remember your face, and they would come to your village at night.

Tumaq knelt. He pressed his forehead to the ground. He spoke in Mi'kmaq: 'I am Tumaq. I am a hunter. I am passing through. I mean no harm.'

The Stone Giant stopped chewing. It turned its head — slowly, like a boulder rolling downhill. It looked at Tumaq. Its eyes were not eyes but shadows in stone, deep and old and patient.

'You are small,' the Stone Giant said. Its voice was the sound of rocks falling in a canyon. 'Everything is small. The trees are small. The mountains are small. Even the glaciers were small, when I was young.'

Tumaq did not look up. 'I am small,' he said. 'But I am here.'

The Stone Giant considered this. 'Yes,' it said. 'You are here. That is something.'

It turned back to its tree. It finished eating. Then it walked away — each step an earthquake, each footfall leaving a crater in the earth. The forest shook. The birds fled. The river changed course.

Tumaq waited until the sound of footsteps faded. Then he stood and walked home. He told the elders what he had seen. They were not surprised.

'The Stone Giants were here before us,' the elders said. 'They will be here after us. They are the mountain's memory. They remember the first sunrise, the first snow, the first hunter who walked this land. We are a moment in their long lives.'

'Will they hurt us?' Tumaq asked.

'Only if we forget them,' the elders said. 'The Stone Giants do not attack. They simply are. But if we forget that they exist, if we stop leaving offerings at the mountain's edge, if we stop speaking their names — then they will remind us. And their reminders are earthquakes.'

Tumaq never forgot. Every spring, he left a bundle of tobacco at the base of the Cobequid Mountains. Every autumn, he sang the stone song — a low, rumbling chant that sounded like the mountain breathing.

And sometimes, on quiet nights, he would hear it: a distant sound, like footsteps, like boulders rolling, like the mountain shifting in its sleep. The Stone Giant, walking through the forest, remembering everything.
moral: The world is older than we are. The spirits who were here first deserve our respect and remembrance.
source: Based on Mi'kmaq oral traditions from the Atlantic provinces of Canada.
